note: Fix it: each problem lists checks in order, easiest and most likely first. 'lesson' links a lesson id; 'dia' is a diagram.

problems.title: A tangle of thread under the fabric
problems.about: A big loopy nest on the underside almost always means the **top** thread isn't in the tension discs, even though it looks like a bobbin problem.

steps.check: Was the presser foot down when you threaded the top thread?
steps.fix: Raise the presser foot (this opens the tension discs) and rethread the whole top thread from the spool. Then lower the foot and test.

steps.check: Did the thread skip the take-up lever?
steps.fix: Turn the handwheel toward you until the lever is at its highest point, then rethread so the thread goes through its eye.

steps.check: Did you hold the thread tails for the first few stitches?
steps.fix: Hold both tails toward the back for the first 2 or 3 stitches, and start with the needle down in the fabric.

steps.check: Is the bobbin in the right way round?
steps.fix: Take it out and drop it back in so the thread unwinds the way your manual shows, then pull it through the little slot until it clicks.

steps.check: Is the thread caught on the spool?
steps.fix: Look for a little notch on the spool's end. Turn the spool so the thread comes off without catching, and add a spool cap if your machine has one.

steps.check: Is the needle old, bent, or the wrong size?
steps.fix: Put in a fresh needle that suits the fabric (80/12 for most cottons, 90/14 or 100/16 for heavy fabric).

steps.check: Is the top tension very high?
steps.fix: Set the tension dial back to the middle (often 4) and test on a scrap.

steps.check: Is the thread old or cheap?
steps.fix: Old thread gets brittle. Tug a length: if it snaps easily, use a new spool of good all-purpose polyester.

steps.check: Is it threaded right?
steps.fix: Rethread from the start with the presser foot up.

problems.title: The needle broke
problems.about: Turn the machine off and find every piece of the broken needle before you go on.

steps.check: Did the needle hit a pin?
steps.fix: Pull pins out just before the needle reaches them. Never sew over them.

steps.check: Were you pulling or pushing the fabric?
steps.fix: Let the feed dogs move the fabric. Your hands only guide it. Pulling bends the needle into the plate.

steps.check: Is the needle too thin for the fabric?
steps.fix: Use a thicker needle for heavy fabric or many layers: a denim 100/16 for canvas and denim.

steps.check: Is the needle pushed all the way up?
steps.fix: Loosen the clamp, push the new needle up as far as it goes with the flat side to the back, and tighten.

steps.check: Is the presser foot on firmly?
steps.fix: A loose foot can knock the needle. Click it back on, and check it's the right foot for the stitch (a straight stitch foot can't zigzag).

steps.check: Is the needle dull, bent, or in backwards?
steps.fix: Put in a fresh needle, pushed all the way up with the flat side to the back.

steps.check: Is it the right kind of needle?
steps.fix: Knits need a ballpoint or stretch needle; thick fabric needs a bigger needle; fine silky fabric needs a Microtex needle.

steps.check: Is the machine threaded right?
steps.fix: Rethread the top with the presser foot up, and check the bobbin.

steps.check: Is the fabric flagging (bouncing up and down with the needle)?
steps.fix: Hold the fabric flat on both sides of the foot, or sew with a strip of tissue paper underneath and tear it away after.

problems.title: Bobbin thread shows on top
problems.about: If you see little dots of bobbin thread on top, the top thread is pulling too hard.

steps.check: Is the top tension too high?
steps.fix: Turn the tension dial to a lower number a little at a time, testing on a scrap after each change.

steps.check: Is the bobbin threaded through its tension spring?
steps.fix: Take the bobbin out and drop it in again, pulling the thread into the slot until it clicks.

steps.check: Are the top and bobbin threads very different?
steps.fix: Use the same thread on top and in the bobbin.

problems.title: Loops on the underside
problems.about: Loops underneath mean the top thread is too loose. Small loops are a tension issue; a big nest is usually a threading issue.

steps.check: Is the top thread in the tension discs?
steps.fix: Rethread with the presser foot UP, then lower it before sewing.

steps.check: Is the top tension too low?
steps.fix: Turn the tension dial up a little at a time, testing on a scrap.

steps.check: Still loopy?
steps.fix: See "A tangle of thread under the fabric": the same fixes apply.

steps.check: Is the presser foot down?
steps.fix: Lower it. Without it, the feed dogs can't grip the fabric.

steps.check: Is the stitch length set to 0?
steps.fix: Set it to 2.5. At 0 the machine sews in place.

steps.check: Are the feed dogs dropped?
steps.fix: Some machines have a switch (often at the back or under the free arm) that lowers them for darning. Raise them again.

steps.check: Is the fabric very thick at the start?
steps.fix: Put a folded scrap of the same thickness behind the foot so it sits level, or start sewing just past the thick part.

problems.title: The machine jams or the handwheel won't turn

steps.check: Is thread caught in the bobbin area?
steps.fix: Turn off the machine. Remove the needle plate (often a screw or two) and the bobbin, and clear out any thread and lint with a small brush.

steps.check: Is the bobbin winder still switched on?
steps.fix: On many machines the needle won't move while the winder is pushed over. Push it back.

steps.check: Did fabric get pulled down into the needle hole?
steps.fix: Cut the threads, lift the fabric free, and start again holding the thread tails. A straight-stitch plate or a scrap 'leader' helps with thin fabric.

problems.title: The needle comes unthreaded as I start

steps.check: Did you stop with the needle at its highest point?
steps.fix: Always stop with the take-up lever at the top (turn the handwheel toward you). Then the first stitch can't pull the thread out.

steps.check: Is the thread tail long enough?
steps.fix: Leave about {{4 in}} of thread behind the needle, and hold it for the first stitches.

steps.check: Is the stitch too long or too short for the fabric?
steps.fix: Try 2.5 mm, or 2 mm for thin fabric. Test on a scrap.

steps.check: Is the top tension too tight?
steps.fix: Lower the tension a little and test.

steps.check: Is the needle dull or too thick?
steps.fix: Put in a fresh needle, one size thinner for light fabric.

steps.check: Are you pulling the fabric?
steps.fix: Let it feed by itself. Your hands just guide.

steps.check: Did you press the seam?
steps.fix: Press the stitching flat first (to 'set' it), then press the seam open or to one side. Many small puckers vanish.

problems.title: Seams come out wavy or stretched

steps.check: Is it a curved or bias edge?
steps.fix: Staystitch curves {{1/2 in}} from the edge right after cutting, and handle bias pieces gently.

steps.check: Is the top layer creeping ahead of the bottom one?
steps.fix: Pin more often, sew slower, or use a walking foot. Lift the foot now and then (needle down) to let the layers relax.

steps.check: Is it a knit?
steps.fix: Use a ballpoint needle and a narrow zigzag, and don't stretch the fabric as you sew. Knits get their own level later.

problems.title: My seam wanders off the line

steps.check: Are you watching the needle?
steps.fix: Watch the fabric edge at the {{SA}} guide line instead. The needle takes care of itself.

steps.check: Is it hard to see the guide line?
steps.fix: Stick a strip of masking tape on the needle plate along the {{SA}} line, or use a magnetic seam guide (not on computerized machines).

steps.check: Are you sewing fast?
steps.fix: Slow down. Steady and slow beats fast and wobbly.

steps.check: Are the seams finished?
steps.fix: Zigzag, pink, or serge the raw edges right after sewing each seam.

steps.check: Is the fabric loosely woven (like linen or gauze)?
steps.fix: Finish edges before you even start sewing, handle the pieces as little as you can, and consider French seams.

steps.check: Did you clip too close?
steps.fix: Clips and notches stop just short of the stitching. If a clip went through, sew a short second row of stitches just inside the first.

steps.check: Did you trim the corner?
steps.fix: Snip the seam allowance off diagonally across the corner, close to (not through) the stitching.

steps.check: Did you push it out gently?
steps.fix: Use a chopstick or point turner, from the inside. Don't poke through.

steps.check: Still bulky?
steps.fix: On thick fabric, take one small stitch straight across the point before pivoting. It gives the fabric room to turn.

steps.check: Is the iron too hot for the fiber?
steps.fix: Turn it down to the right setting for the fabric (see the Fabric guide), and test on a scrap.

steps.check: Did you press on the right side?
steps.fix: Press from the wrong side, or use a pressing cloth (a piece of plain cotton or silk organza) between the iron and fabric.

steps.check: Can it be rescued?
steps.fix: On wool, steam held just above the mark (iron not touching) and a light brush can lift some shine. Synthetic shine is usually permanent.

problems.title: Seam ridges show through on the front

steps.check: Are the seam allowances pressing a print onto the front?
steps.fix: Slip strips of paper (or envelope card) under the seam allowances while pressing.

steps.check: Are you sliding the iron?
steps.fix: Press: lift, set down, hold, lift. Sliding pushes ridges into the fabric.
